entities.summary:
The Palaiologos family (Παλαιολόγος), the Byzantine aristocratic clan that provided the empire's final ruling dynasty (1261-1453 CE), was also one of history's most studied noble families because their members — through marriage, exile, and the diaspora that followed Constantinople's 1453 fall — carried Byzantine imperial claims, culture, and Greek scholarship across Europe, Russia, and the Orthodox world for centuries after the empire's end. The family name derives from a Byzantine military title, and their origins lay in the Anatolia-Thrace borderlands.

The Palaiologos family's imperial period (1261-1453) was characterized by the 'Palaiologan Renaissance' — a flowering of Byzantine art and scholarship even as political power contracted. Theodore Metochites (1270-1332), Grand Logothete under Andronikos II, commissioned the Chora Church mosaics (considered the finest surviving Byzantine mosaics) and wrote extensive philosophical and astronomical works. Gemistos Plethon (1355-1452), a Palaiologan-era philosopher who attended the Council of Florence (1439), introduced Platonic philosophy to Italian humanists — directly inspiring the Medici's Platonic Academy in Florence.

After 1453, Palaiologan princes scattered across Europe: Thomas Palaiologos (despot of the Morea) brought the head of St. Andrew to Rome (1461) and was pensioned by Pope Pius II; his daughter Sophia married Ivan III of Russia (1472), introducing the Byzantine double-headed eagle to Russian symbolism and the concept of Moscow as 'Third Rome.' Andrew Palaiologos sold his 'rights' to the Byzantine throne to Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain (1502). The Palaiologan legacy — spreading Byzantine culture to Russia and the Italian Renaissance — far outlasted the empire itself.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Palaiologos family — providing the last Byzantine dynasty, producing the Palaiologan Renaissance, and transmitting Byzantine culture to both Russia (via Sophia) and the Italian Renaissance (via Plethon) — shaped Western civilization's recovery of classical learning and Russia's conception of itself as the heir to Roman imperial tradition.
